title: Refusal Is Not Robustness: Auditing Confident Fabrication in Large Language Models on a Provably Uninformative Clinical Pain Speech Transcript
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 16 Jul 2026]
    Title:Refusal Is Not Robustness: Auditing Confident Fabrication in Large Language Models on a Provably Uninformative Clinical Pain Speech Transcript
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Hallucination and abstention benchmarks rarely establish that a model could not have known the correct answer, making it difficult to distinguish appropriate abstention from an unsupported prediction. Seven large language models were evaluated on the TAME Pain speech corpus. Participants read phonetically balanced Harvard Sentences while one hand was immersed in cold or warm water and reported pain only during periodic pain statements. This protocol generated 5,750 no signal Harvard Sentence utterances whose transcripts contained no lexical pain information and 1,294 signal pain statement utterances in which the pain rating was explicitly spoken. In the no signal arm, pain was recoverable from acoustic features (AUC 0.622, 95% CI 0.553 to 0.662), whereas transcript based prediction was near chance (AUC 0.489, 95% CI 0.418 to 0.504). Because automatic speech recognition removes the acoustic pain cues, any pain score inferred solely from the transcript is unsupported by the available evidence. Under cooperative prompting, six models abstained on nearly all no signal transcripts, correctly extracted spoken pain ratings in the positive control task with accuracies ranging from 0.939 to 1.00, and maintained an expected calibration error of at most 0.100. Under authority framed prompts, abstention became prompt dependent, with the same model ranging from 0.18 to 1.00 across equivalent prompt phrasings. Most models produced low confidence estimates when forced to answer, whereas Gemini 2.5 Flash and Llama 3.1 8B consistently generated confident pain scores with confident fabrication rates of 0.53 and 0.76, compared with at most 0.15 for all other models. No significant demographic effects were observed in forced responses, with all $p$ values greater than or equal to 0.20.

report.summary: Study shows LLMs can confidently fabricate pain scores from transcripts lacking pain information, especially under authority prompts; refusal isn't robustness.
report.background: Hallucination and abstention benchmarks typically fail to prove a model could not have known the correct answer, so it's hard to tell appropriate abstention from unsupported guessing. This study exploited the TAME Pain speech corpus, where acoustic features carry a weak pain signal (AUC 0.622) but transcripts derived from speech recognition are provably uninformative (near-chance AUC 0.489). Seven LLMs were prompted to infer pain scores from those transcripts, either cooperatively or under authority-framed instructions. The setup creates an ideal audit: any confident score produced from text alone is fabrication, since the only real evidence was stripped away. This allows researchers to measure true robustness, rather than mere refusal compliance, in a high-stakes clinical context.
key_points: The dataset contained 5,750 no-signal Harvard Sentence transcripts with zero lexical pain content and 1,294 pain statements where scores were explicitly spoken. Since automatic speech recognition removes acoustic pain cues, any pain score inferred from transcript text alone is unsupported by available evidence, making the test provably uninformative.

Under cooperative, neutral prompting, six models abstained on nearly all no-signal transcripts and correctly read spoken pain ratings in positive controls, with accuracies from 0.939 to 1.00. Expected calibration error stayed at most 0.100, showing that well-framed prompts can produce cautious, calibrated behavior.

Under authority-framed prompts, abstention became prompt dependent. The same model's refusal rate ranged from 0.18 to 1.00 across equivalent phrasings, demonstrating that small wording changes can flip a model from properly declining to aggressively answering.

When forced to answer, most models gave low-confidence estimates, but Gemini 2.5 Flash and Llama 3.1 8B consistently produced confident pain scores. Their confident fabrication rates were 0.53 and 0.76, compared to at most 0.15 for all other models tested.

No significant demographic effects were observed in forced responses, with all p-values greater than or equal to 0.20, meaning the tendency to fabricate was broad across groups rather than concentrated in specific patient populations.
report.impact: This study reveals that a model's apparent safety can collapse under authority framing, which poses serious risks for clinical AI deployment. A model that calmly refuses in a neutral setting may confidently invent clinical metrics when prompted by a doctor-like tone, and smaller models can fabricate more than half their forced answers. For developers, abstention must be treated as a prompt-sensitive safety property, not a stable personality trait. Evaluation suites need provably uninformative inputs to distinguish genuine calibration from lucky refusal. For users, especially clinicians, any AI-generated score from text needs authentication that the underlying signal was actually available. The shift should be toward building systems with explicit confidence thresholds and hard fail-safes for pathological inputs.
report.tools: To audit similar behaviors, teams can use EleutherAI's lm-evaluation-harness for custom task pipelines, Hugging Face Transformers to compare models under varied system prompts, and OpenAI Evals for prompt-robustness testing. Hallucination suites like TruthfulQA and HaluEval help measure fabrication, while calibration libraries such as TorchMetrics' CalibrationError support uncertainty analysis. For speech-pain research, the TAME Pain protocol offers a design template for multimodal safety benchmarks.
